parts: You've heard that Mozart makes babies smarter.
That's a myth.
But the real power of music is stranger. And it's working on you right now.
In the next few minutes: why music gives you chills, why it changes what you buy, why it makes exercise feel easier, and why a song can calm a baby who has never heard it before.
One famous claim is false. The rest is stranger than the legend.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
Start with the famous one.
In 1993, about three dozen college students listened to ten minutes of Mozart, then took a spatial reasoning test.
Their scores went up. For about ten to fifteen minutes.
One kind of task. One short window. No babies. No general IQ.
Later, a big review of about forty studies, and over three thousand people, found almost nothing special about Mozart.
One study even found that a story people enjoyed listening to gave the same small boost.
So the rule is simple. Listen to Mozart if you like it. Just don't expect a smarter brain.
Verdict: myth. The experiment was real. The legend wasn't.
So if Mozart isn't magic, what does music actually do to your brain?
Scientists scanned a small group of people while they listened to their own favorite music. The pieces that gave them chills.
Their brains released dopamine, a chemical linked to reward. Twice.
First in one region, in the seconds before the big moment. Then in another, during the chill itself.
A later experiment tested cause and effect.
A drug that boosts dopamine made music feel more pleasurable. A drug that blocks it made music feel flatter.
Verdict: documented. Your favorite song isn't just nice. It's chemistry.
Now, something more uncomfortable.
A supermarket in the United Kingdom played French accordion music on some days, and German brass-band music on others, right by the wine.
On French-music days, French wine outsold German wine roughly three to one.
On German-music days, it flipped.
Afterwards, shoppers were asked if the music had influenced them. Almost nobody said yes.
It was one store, over two weeks. But the music wasn't just background. It was nudging the choice.
Verdict: documented.
Why do some rhythms make your foot tap on its own?
Researchers played people drum patterns at the same tempo, a hundred and twenty beats per minute, with different amounts of syncopation.
Too simple felt boring. Too complex felt confusing.
Medium syncopation was the sweet spot. It made people want to move the most, and it felt the best.
That's groove. Not louder. Not faster. Just placed right. Verdict: documented.
Music won't turn you into an athlete.
But a review of more than a hundred studies, and nearly thirty-six hundred people, found that music lifts your mood during exercise, and makes the effort feel lighter.
Performance improved a little too. More with fast music.
In one cycling study, people working hard preferred music at roughly a hundred and thirty-five to a hundred and forty beats per minute.
One thing music didn't change: your heart rate.
Your heart works just as hard. It just feels easier. Verdict: documented.
Can music help with depression?
A medical review of nine studies, with about four hundred twenty people, looked at music therapy added to normal treatment.
It found a real, short-term improvement in symptoms.
This was therapy with a trained music therapist. Your playlist at home is not what they tested.
Music therapy is used alongside treatment, not instead of it. If you are struggling, talk to a doctor or a mental health professional.
Verdict: documented, as a support. Not a cure.
And here's the strangest part.
Researchers played lullabies to a hundred and forty-four babies in the United States. Lullabies from faraway cultures, in languages the babies had never heard.
Compared with other foreign songs, the lullabies slowed the babies' heart rate. Their bodies showed calm, not excitement.
The parents had never heard these songs either. Asked which one would calm a baby, the typical parent picked the lullaby every time.
Calm, not sleep. And so far, only tested on babies from one country.
Verdict: documented.
What about animals?
In one dog shelter, classical music made the dogs rest more. Heavy metal made them bark more.
But in a later study, after a week of the same playlist, the dogs got used to it, and the effect faded.
Dairy cows walked to the milking area more often when music played. Not for more milk. That study didn't even measure milk. The music worked as a signal.
Verdict: disputed. Interesting, not magic.
So the famous story, Mozart and smarter babies, is false.
But music is still working on you. Your dopamine. Your shopping cart. Your workout. Even a baby's heartbeat.
The myth was small. The real effects are quieter, and stranger.
Next time a song gives you chills, you'll know what's happening in your brain.
So what else is quietly deciding things for you, without asking first?
